name: Kantowski-Sachs Cosmologies
description: The spatially homogeneous, anisotropic cosmologies outside Bianchi's classification. Every moment of time is a cylinder $\mathbb{R} \times S^2$, or $S^1 \times S^2$, whose length and whose spheres evolve separately, and the vacuum member is the region inside the horizon of a Schwarzschild black hole.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: A universe is spatially homogeneous when a group of motions carries any point of a moment of time to any other, and Luigi Bianchi's classification of 1898 lists the groups of three parameters that do so with exactly one motion for each pair of points [bianchi1898, ellismaccallum1969]. A group of four parameters acting on the same three dimensional moments also makes them homogeneous, and one such group contains none of Bianchi's acting simply transitively [kantowski1966, ellismaccallum1969]. George Ellis and Malcolm MacCallum called its cosmology in 1969 "the only fluid solution in which a group of motions multiply transitive on spacelike three-surfaces does not have a subgroup $G_3$ simply transitive in these surfaces" [ellismaccallum1969]. The group is $\mathbb{R} \times SO(3)$, the translations along an axis together with the rotations of a sphere, and each moment it acts on has the topology $\mathbb{R} \times S^2$ [ashtekar2006].¶B. Datt had met a relative of it in Calcutta in 1938, a spherically symmetric solution for dust in which the radius of every sphere depends on time alone, and set it aside as of little physical significance; it is an inhomogeneous generalization of the dust cosmology of this family [datt1938, krasinski1999datt]. Aleksandr Kompaneets and A. S. Chernov were the first to study this spacetime, in 1964 [kompaneets1964, conradi1995]. They looked for a universe whose matter is distributed homogeneously and whose metric is anisotropic, in a comoving synchronous frame $ds^2 = dt^2 - e^{\nu}dr^2 - e^{\omega}d\varphi^2 - e^{\mu}dz^2$ in which nothing depends on $z$ [kompaneets1964]. The field equations allowed three types of solution, $e^{\omega/2} = e^{\nu/2}h(r)$ with $h = \sin\sigma r$, $h = r$, or $h = \sinh\sigma r$, a model closed, quasi-Euclidean, or open in $r$ [kompaneets1964].¶The closed type, whose surfaces of $r$ and $\varphi$ are spheres, has no simply transitive group of three parameters [kantowski1966, ellismaccallum1969]. The types with plane and hyperbolic symmetry are of Bianchi types I and III [ellismaccallum1969, mengual2026]. Kompaneets and Chernov solved the equations for dust and for an ultrarelativistic gas with $\varepsilon = 3p$, and showed that the singularity in time of the anisotropic model differs from that of the isotropic Friedmann-Lemaître model [kompaneets1964].¶Ronald Kantowski and Rainer Sachs found the same cosmologies independently of Kompaneets and Chernov, and gave the solutions for a dust source in explicit form in 1966 [kantowski1966, conradi1995]. They characterized them as "those spatially homogeneous expanding models that do not permit a simply transitive three-parameter group of motions" [kantowski1966]. They compared the models in detail with observations and with the Friedmann models, and in a few instances obtained time scales slightly longer than those of the corresponding Friedmann models [kantowski1966].¶The member of the family with no matter is, in Ellis and MacCallum's words, "the spatially homogeneous part of the Schwarzschild solution" [ellismaccallum1969]. Inside the horizon of a Schwarzschild black hole the areal radius is a time and Schwarzschild's $t$ measures length along the axis, so that with $T$ for the radius and $r$ for $ct$ the metric is $ds^2 = -dT^2/(r_s/T - 1) + (r_s/T - 1)\,dr^2 + T^2d\Omega^2$, the Kantowski-Sachs metric with $b = T$ and $a^2 = r_s/T - 1$ [doran2008]. The geometry has two types of singularity, cigarlike where $b \to 0$ and disklike where $a \to 0$ [conradi1995]. Without matter the disklike singularity, which is the horizon, is a coordinate singularity [conradi1995, doran2008]. With dust the matter density becomes infinite there and the curvature diverges [conradi1995].¶C. B. Collins worked out the global structure of the family in 1977, defining it by a four parameter isometry group that acts on spacelike hypersurfaces and has a three parameter subgroup whose orbits are 2-surfaces of constant curvature [collins1977]. He described the models as "nonempty analogs of part of the extended Schwarzschild manifold" [collins1977]. Every such model whose matter is a perfect fluid satisfying reasonable energy conditions is geodesically incomplete both to the past and to the future, and the energy density of the fluid is infinite at each singularity [collins1977]. For a fluid with a barotropic equation of state the field equations decouple to form a plane autonomous system, from which Collins drew phase plane diagrams of the energy density and the shear anisotropy, and diagrams of the conformal structure of these universes [collins1977]. Edmond Weber added a cosmological constant in 1984 and found a set of solutions of nonzero measure that become isotropic in an infinite cosmological time [weber1984].¶Raymond Laflamme and Paul Shellard studied the wave function of the universe defined by the Hartle-Hawking proposal on the Kantowski-Sachs minisuperspace in 1987 [laflamme1987]. Most of its classical trajectories recollapse to a singularity, and the universes "generically evolve from isotropy during expansion to increasing anisotropy during recollapse, ending as a black-hole interior" [laflamme1987]. Abhay Ashtekar and Martin Bojowald foliated the region inside the Schwarzschild horizon in 2006 by slices invariant under the Kantowski-Sachs group, which let them carry the techniques of homogeneous quantum cosmology over to the black hole [ashtekar2006]. The quantum geometry effects that resolve the classical singularity in homogeneous cosmologies resolve the Schwarzschild singularity as well [ashtekar2006]. The perfect fluid solutions of Kompaneets, Chernov, Kantowski, and Sachs describe a thermodynamic perfect fluid in isentropic evolution, as Salvador Mengual and Joan Josep Ferrando showed in 2026 [mengual2026].

related.text: The vacuum member of the family is the inside of Schwarzschild's horizon, where $r$ is a time [ellismaccallum1969, doran2008].
Every other spatially homogeneous cosmology. The Kantowski-Sachs group has four parameters, and none of Bianchi's groups sits inside it acting simply transitively [kantowski1966, ellismaccallum1969].
Peter Szekeres's dust cosmologies of 1975 hold the Kantowski-Sachs dust models in their second class, and in general have no Killing vector [szekeres1975, bonnor1977].
With its axis wrapped into a circle, the member with no matter is a polarised Gowdy spacetime on $S^2 \times S^1$ [obregon1998].
A regular black hole whose inside, where $r$ is a time, is a Kantowski-Sachs cosmology that bounces: its spheres shrink to a least radius $a$ and grow again [bronnikov2022].
A white hole holds the vacuum member with its spheres growing: it is the space between the singularity and the dust that comes out of it [novikov1965].
Kantowski and Sachs's dust universe with the stretch along its axis free to differ from shell to shell, found by B. Datt in 1938 and again by Vladimir Ruban in 1968 [datt1938, ruban1968].
The inflating region of Gott and Li's universe, de Sitter space identified under a boost, with $a = \sinh(ct/r_0)$ and $b = r_0\cosh(ct/r_0)$ for the de Sitter radius $r_0$ [gott1998].

The geometry of the no-boundary proposal on the round minisuperspace, half a 4-sphere joined to de Sitter's waist [hartle1983]. Laflamme and Shellard carried the proposal over to the Kantowski-Sachs minisuperspace [laflamme1987].

coordinates.name: Comoving

parameters.description: Scale factor along $r$, the axis of the cylinder ($a > 0$), dimensionless
Radius of the spheres, a length ($b > 0$); $a$ and $b$ are independent

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ a cosmic time, $r$ a comoving length along the axis of the cylinder, and $\theta$ and $\phi$ angles on the spheres. The scale factor $a(t)$ is dimensionless and the radius $b(t)$ of the spheres is a length, both free functions of $t$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, a prime is the derivative along that chart time, $a' = da/d(ct)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Vacuum (Schwarzschild Interior)
coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(T, r, \theta, \phi)$, where the time $T$ is the areal radius of the spheres, a length, and $r$ is $c$ times Schwarzschild's $t$, a length along the axis of the cylinder. In the comoving chart $a = \sqrt{r_s/T - 1}$, $b = T$, and $c\,dt = dT/a$.

coordinates.name: Dust, Parametric Time

parameters.description: Largest radius the spheres reach, at $\eta = 0$, a length
Dimensionless constant with $|\kappa| < \pi/2$; the model is symmetric in time about $\eta = 0$ where $\kappa = 0$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(\eta, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $\eta$ a dimensionless time and $r$ a comoving length along the axis of the cylinder. In the comoving chart $a = 1 + (\eta + \kappa)\tan\eta$, $b = b_0\cos^2\eta$, and $c\,dt = 2b_0\cos^2\eta\,d\eta$, so $ct = b_0\left(\eta + \sin\eta\cos\eta\right)$. The dust is at rest in the chart, with density $\rho = \dfrac{c^2}{8\pi G\,a\,b^2}$.
